questions.question: What are virtual threads in Java 21 (Project Loom)? How do they differ from platform threads?
questions.title: Virtual Threads in Java 21 — Project Loom Explained
questions.direct_answer: **Virtual threads** (JEP 444, Java 21 GA) are lightweight, JVM-managed threads that let you write simple **one-thread-per-request** blocking code while scaling to **millions** of concurrent threads. They **look and feel identical to `java.lang.Thread`** (they *are* subclasses) but are scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of **carrier threads** (by default, `ForkJoinPool` sized to CPUs). When a virtual thread hits a blocking I/O call (socket read, HTTP, JDBC), the JVM **unmounts** it from the carrier — stack gets parked on the heap, carrier goes to serve another virtual thread. The memory cost is **kilobytes, not megabytes** — a platform thread's 1 MB default stack becomes a resizable heap object. Create them with `Thread.ofVirtual().start(task)` or `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`. The goal: **kill thread pools for I/O-bound server code** and let you write straight-line blocking logic without callback hell or reactive complexity.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can articulate what virtual threads change (cheap blocking I/O), how they're scheduled (carrier threads, unmount on block), and when they apply vs don't (I/O-bound yes, CPU-bound no)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking virtual threads make CPU-bound code faster (they don't — still limited by CPUs). Or assuming you should now use them everywhere, including synchronized-heavy code where pinning causes carrier exhaustion
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the mount/unmount model concretely, mention pinning on synchronized and native frames, note that ThreadLocal is 'fine but heavy' for millions of threads (ScopedValue alternative), and that the whole point is eliminating the need for reactive frameworks for typical request-handler code

sections.title: The Problem Virtual Threads Solve
How Virtual Threads Are Scheduled
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph App[Application] VT1[Virtual
Thread 1] VT2[Virtual
Thread 2] VTn[Virtual
Thread N
millions] end subgraph Sched[JVM Scheduler
ForkJoinPool carrier threads] C1[Carrier 1] C2[Carrier 2] C3[Carrier 3
sized to CPUs] end subgraph OS[Operating System] T1[OS thread] T2[OS thread] T3[OS thread] end VT1 -- mount/unmount --> C1 VT2 -- mount/unmount --> C2 VTn -- mount/unmount --> C3 C1 --> T1 C2 --> T2 C3 --> T3 VT1 -. blocked I/O:
park stack to heap .-> VT1 ``` **Key flow**: 1. `Thread.ofVirtual().start(task)` creates a virtual thread; task starts running. 2. JVM **mounts** the virtual thread on a carrier (platform thread); task runs normally. 3. Task calls blocking I/O (`Socket.read`, `HttpClient.send`, JDBC). 4. JVM **unmounts** the virtual thread: copies its stack to the heap, frees the carrier. 5. Carrier picks up another virtual thread to run. 6. When I/O completes, JVM schedules the virtual thread back onto any available carrier; stack is restored. Number of carriers = `Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()` by default. Virtual threads share these. The parallelism equals CPU count; the concurrency equals however many virtual threads you can fit in heap.

sections.title: Virtual Threads vs Platform Threads
sections.content:
| Dimension | Platform Thread | Virtual Thread |
|---|---|---|
| **Backed by** | OS kernel thread | JVM scheduling onto carrier |
| **Stack size** | 1 MB default (fixed) | Resizable, starts ~KB, stored on heap |
| **Creation cost** | ~1 ms, syscall | ~microseconds, pure Java |
| **Memory per thread** | ~1 MB | ~few KB (varies with stack depth) |
| **Max practical count** | ~thousands (5K-10K) | **Millions** |
| **Scheduling** | Preemptive by OS kernel | Cooperative by JVM at blocking points |
| **Blocking I/O** | OS parks the thread | JVM unmounts, carrier reused |
| **Parallelism** | Limited by OS thread count | Parallelism = carriers; concurrency = virtual threads |
| **ThreadLocal** | Works normally | Works but heavy at scale — prefer `ScopedValue` |
| **`synchronized` blocks** | Normal | **Pins** to carrier — can starve other virtual threads |
| **Good for** | CPU-bound; small fixed count | I/O-bound; high concurrency |

sections.title: Creating and Using Virtual Threads
What Makes Them 'Virtual' — The Mount/Unmount Mechanism
sections.content:
The magic is in the JDK's instrumentation of blocking operations. All `java.net`, `java.nio`, `java.io`, `java.util.concurrent` (parking), and `JDBC` drivers written in Java have been updated so that when they block:

1. They call an internal `Continuation.yield()` which **captures the current stack** of the virtual thread.
2. The stack is stored as a heap object (essentially a linked list of frames).
3. The carrier thread is released — it goes back to the scheduler pool.
4. When the I/O completes (kernel `epoll`/`kqueue` fires), the virtual thread is added back to the scheduler's run queue.
5. An available carrier picks it up — a `Continuation.run()` restores the stack onto that carrier.
6. Execution resumes at the blocking point as if nothing happened.

This works automatically for all instrumented blocking calls in the JDK. Third-party libraries using `java.net.Socket` or `java.nio.channels` inherit the benefit for free.

**Key consequence**: number of concurrent I/O operations is bounded by **heap memory and file descriptors**, not thread count. A 4 GB heap easily supports a million parked virtual threads.

sections.title: What Virtual Threads Don't Change
sections.content:
Important things to keep realistic:

- **CPU parallelism is unchanged.** If you have 8 cores, you can execute 8 things at once, virtual or not. Virtual threads help concurrency (many tasks overlapping), not parallelism (many tasks computing simultaneously).
- **CPU-bound work doesn't benefit.** A virtual thread running a tight loop monopolizes its carrier just like a platform thread would. Use the traditional `ForkJoinPool` for compute-bound work.
- **`synchronized` blocks pin**: while inside a `synchronized` block/method, the virtual thread cannot be unmounted. Blocking I/O inside `synchronized` holds the carrier. At scale this causes **carrier exhaustion**. Fix: migrate to `ReentrantLock`, which doesn't pin.
- **Native frames pin**: JNI calls also prevent unmounting while on-stack. Not usually a problem unless you have heavy native code.
- **Pooling doesn't make sense.** Don't put virtual threads in a fixed pool — defeats the purpose. New-thread-per-task is the pattern.
- **Debugger support is good** — virtual threads show up in thread dumps and your IDE, labeled appropriately. But a dump of a million threads takes a while; Java 21 added `jcmd Thread.dump_to_file` for the new format.
- **`ThreadLocal` works** — but each virtual thread carrying its own copy of a large ThreadLocal becomes expensive at 1M threads. Use **`ScopedValue`** (Java 21 preview, stable in later versions) for immutable per-scope values.

sections.title: When to Use Virtual Threads
sections.content:
**Great fit**:
- **HTTP servers, REST APIs, JDBC-heavy backend services** — classic one-thread-per-request patterns now scale to millions.
- **Outbound I/O fan-out** — submitting hundreds/thousands of parallel HTTP calls.
- **Message consumers** — each message processed on its own virtual thread.
- **Migration target from reactive frameworks** — if your code is already async-blocking via `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync` for I/O, virtual threads often simplify it.

**Bad fit**:
- **CPU-bound work** (image processing, math, parsing). Use `ForkJoinPool` or a fixed platform-thread pool sized to CPUs.
- **Heavy `synchronized` code** that blocks on I/O inside the lock — pinning exhausts carriers. Refactor first.
- **Code with huge ThreadLocal footprint** — migrate to ScopedValue or explicit parameter passing.
- **Existing high-throughput systems on Netty/WebFlux that already work** — don't rewrite. Loom is for simplifying, not micro-optimizing.

**Watch out for**:
- **Thread pool config that no longer applies**: if you were using `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200)` to limit concurrency to protect a downstream, that limit is gone with virtual threads. Use a `Semaphore` instead.
- **Downstream saturation** — a million virtual threads can easily overwhelm a downstream DB/API that was previously protected by your small thread pool.
- **Monitoring** — tools like JFR have virtual-thread events; `jstack` still works but output is different. Update your dashboards.
- **Library compatibility** — most modern JDKs/libraries are aware; older JDBC drivers or native-heavy libraries may pin.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Virtual threads** (Java 21 GA, JEP 444) are lightweight threads scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of **carrier threads**.
- Subclasses of `java.lang.Thread` — same API, no new programming model.
- Create with **`Thread.ofVirtual().start()`**, **`Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`**, or **`Thread.startVirtualThread()`**.
- Blocking I/O **unmounts** the virtual thread (stack parked on heap); carrier serves others. Completion remounts.
- Memory: **KB not MB** — millions are feasible.
- **Carriers = CPUs** by default (`ForkJoinPool`); parallelism unchanged, concurrency massively increased.
- **Pinning** on `synchronized` and native frames — use `ReentrantLock` to avoid carrier exhaustion.
- **Not for CPU-bound work** — virtual threads don't add CPU parallelism.
- **Don't pool them** — create one per task.
- **`ScopedValue`** replaces `ThreadLocal` for scale; `StructuredTaskScope` is the companion for structured concurrency.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Virtual threads are Java 21's Project Loom feature that lets you write **simple blocking code that scales to millions of concurrent threads**.

**The problem they solve**
- Traditional platform threads cost ~1 MB of stack each; you run out around 5K-10K
- For high concurrency, teams were forced into async/reactive frameworks (Netty, Reactor, WebFlux)
- Async comes with callback hell, `CompletableFuture` chains, broken ThreadLocals, unreadable stack traces
- Virtual threads let you go back to one-thread-per-request blocking code — but scale like async

**The mechanism**
- Virtual threads are subclasses of `java.lang.Thread` — same API
- Scheduled by the JVM onto a pool of **carrier threads** (platform threads sized to your CPUs)
- When a virtual thread hits blocking I/O, the JVM **unmounts** it:
  - Stack copied to the heap
  - Carrier freed to run another virtual thread
  - I/O completion reschedules the virtual thread back onto any carrier
- All blocking operations in the JDK (sockets, HttpClient, JDBC) are instrumented
- Transparent to the code you write

**Numbers**
- Memory: from ~1 MB per platform thread down to ~few KB per virtual thread
- Count: thousands → **millions** on typical hardware
- Parallelism unchanged = CPU count
- Concurrency limit = heap memory, not thread count

**How to create**
- `Thread.ofVirtual().start(task)` — builder
- `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` — idiomatic executor form
- `Thread.startVirtualThread(runnable)` — one-liner
- Never pool them — creation is microseconds

**What doesn't change**
- CPU-bound work doesn't get faster — still capped at CPU count
- Don't use virtual threads for tight loops or heavy computation

**Known limitations**
- **Pinning**: `synchronized` blocks and native frames prevent unmounting. Blocking I/O inside synchronized holds a carrier. At scale this causes carrier starvation. Fix: migrate to `ReentrantLock`
- **ThreadLocal**: works fine functionally but millions of threads each carrying their own copy is expensive. Use `ScopedValue` (Java 21 preview) for immutable per-scope values
- **Downstream saturation**: a million virtual threads can easily overwhelm a DB previously protected by a small thread pool. Use Semaphore for flow control

**Good fits**
- HTTP servers, REST APIs, JDBC-heavy backends
- Message consumers, outbound fan-out calls
- Migration target from reactive code that was async-for-blocking-I/O

**Bad fits**
- CPU-bound work (use ForkJoinPool)
- Heavy synchronized code blocking on I/O (refactor first)
- Working WebFlux/Netty systems (don't rewrite for the sake of it)

**Recommendation:** For any **new server-side Java project** dealing with I/O-bound workloads — REST APIs, message handlers, outbound HTTP fan-out — start with **`Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`** and simple blocking code. You get reactive-level scaling without reactive complexity. **Audit existing code for `synchronized` blocks that wrap blocking I/O** and migrate those to `ReentrantLock` before switching — otherwise pinning will bite you under load. Keep a **`Semaphore`-based admission control** for downstream protection, since the implicit rate limiting of small thread pools no longer exists. For CPU-bound code, keep using traditional thread pools. Virtual threads aren't a silver bullet — they're the right tool specifically for high-concurrency blocking I/O, and they're now the **default choice** there.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Virtual threads make thread-per-request viable by making threads cheap — ~1KB initial stack, JVM-scheduled onto a small pool of carrier threads.

**How they work:**
- When a virtual thread calls blocking I/O, it unmounts from the carrier — the carrier is freed for other virtual threads
- Millions can run concurrently; JVM manages scheduling; carrier pool defaults to N = number of CPU cores

**Carrier pinning (main migration concern):**
- `synchronized` block pins the virtual thread to its carrier — cannot unmount during the block
- If the block contains I/O, that carrier thread is wasted — effectively a blocking platform thread again
- Fix: replace `synchronized` with `ReentrantLock` on I/O-heavy paths

**Migration guidelines:**
- Do not pool virtual threads — pooling defeats the purpose; use `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`
- `ThreadLocal` works but risks memory waste with millions of threads — ScopedValue is the replacement
- Enable `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short` during testing to find `synchronized` blocks that need migration

I recommend virtual threads for I/O-heavy workloads like HTTP servers and database-heavy services. CPU-bound computation still benefits from platform threads with ForkJoinPool.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**Virtual threads** (JEP 444, Java 21 GA) are lightweight, JVM-managed threads that let you write simple **one-thread-per-request** blocking code while scaling to **millions** of concurrent threads.

They **look and feel identical to `java.lang.Thread`** (they *are* subclasses) but are scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of **carrier threads** (by default, `ForkJoinPool` sized to CPUs).

When a virtual thread hits a blocking I/O call (socket read, HTTP, JDBC), the JVM **unmounts** it from the carrier — stack gets parked on the heap, carrier goes to serve another virtual thread. The memory cost is **kilobytes, not megabytes** — a platform thread's 1 MB default stack becomes a resizable heap object. Create them with `Thread.ofVirtual().start(task)` or `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`. The goal: **kill thread pools for I/O-bound server code** and let you write straight-line blocking logic without callback hell or reactive complexity.

**Pinning** is when a virtual thread **cannot be unmounted** from its carrier — usually because it's inside a **`synchronized` block** or executing a **native (JNI) frame**. While pinned, any blocking I/O holds the carrier thread, defeating the whole point of Loom. If many virtual threads pin simultaneously on blocking I/O, carriers get **exhausted**: no virtual thread can run because there's no free carrier.

sections.title: Carrier Pinning and the synchronized-to-ReentrantLock Migration
The Classic Pinning Bug
Important trade-off
sections.content: **Use virtual threads when your workload is I/O-bound and high-concurrency** — HTTP servers, REST APIs with DB/downstream calls, message consumers, fan-out client calls. They **eliminate the thread-pool sizing dance** and let you write simple blocking code that scales to millions of concurrent requests. **Do NOT use virtual threads for CPU-bound work** — image processing, heavy parsing, math. They don't add CPU parallelism; you're still capped by core count. Also avoid them when your code holds **`synchronized` locks across blocking I/O** (pinning starves carriers) or when you rely on **heavy `ThreadLocal` state** that would multiply across millions of threads. The mental model: virtual threads are for **scaling blocking I/O**; platform threads / `ForkJoinPool` are for **scaling computation**. On Java 21+, default to virtual threads for request handlers and migrate platform thread pools selectively.

sections.title: The Decision Framework
sections.content:
The guiding question is simple: **does your workload spend most of its time waiting on I/O, or computing?**

- **Waiting** — database queries, HTTP calls, message queue reads, file I/O, socket reads, sleep, await. Virtual threads shine here because the JVM can unmount them during waits and free the carrier for others.
- **Computing** — tight loops, JSON parsing, encryption, image manipulation, serialization. Virtual threads don't help; you still need one CPU core per parallel computation. Use a traditional `ForkJoinPool` or fixed platform-thread pool sized to cores.

**Typical server workloads are overwhelmingly I/O-bound**: a request handler spends 2-5 ms in CPU and 50-200 ms waiting on DB/downstream. That ratio is exactly what virtual threads target.

On Java 21+, the default for new server code should be: **virtual threads for request dispatch and async I/O fan-out, platform threads for CPU pools**.

sections.title: Good Fit vs Bad Fit Scenarios
sections.content:
| Workload | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **REST API handling 10K req/s, each making 3 DB + 2 HTTP calls** | ✅ Perfect | I/O-dominated; blocking code is simpler than reactive |
| **Message consumer reading from Kafka, processing, writing to DB** | ✅ Great | Each message = one virtual thread; blocking I/O throughout |
| **gRPC client making 1000 parallel outbound calls** | ✅ Great | Classic fan-out |
| **File processor reading/writing large files** | ⚠️ Depends | Good if I/O dominates; bad if mostly parsing/encoding CPU |
| **JSON parser transforming 1 GB of data** | ❌ Bad | Pure CPU; use platform thread pool = CPU count |
| **Image thumbnail service** | ❌ Bad | Pure CPU work; no benefit |
| **Encryption batch job** | ❌ Bad | CPU-bound |
| **Legacy code with `synchronized` methods calling JDBC** | ⚠️ Audit first | Pinning will starve carriers; migrate to ReentrantLock first |
| **Code with 50+ MB of ThreadLocal state per thread** | ❌ Bad without refactoring | Millions of copies explode heap; use ScopedValue |
| **Existing Netty/WebFlux app at scale** | ⚠️ Don't rewrite | Already works; migration cost > benefit |

sections.title: The Classic Sweet Spot — Thread-Per-Request Web Servers
sections.content:
Java web servers traditionally face a choice:

- **Tomcat / Jetty with a 200-thread pool** — simple code, but scales to ~200 concurrent slow requests. A slow downstream stalls the whole server.
- **Netty / WebFlux with 8 event-loop threads** — scales to 100K+ connections, but reactive code is complex.

Virtual threads let you keep the simple model and still scale:

```java
// Spring Boot 3.2+
spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true
```

Behind the scenes, Tomcat's request executor becomes a virtual-thread-per-task executor. Your `@RestController` code is unchanged — still blocking JDBC, still blocking `RestTemplate`. But now you can handle 10K+ concurrent slow requests instead of 200.

**Concrete example**: a service that calls 3 downstream APIs per request (each 100 ms).
- Platform threads (200-thread pool): max ~2000 req/s before queueing.
- Virtual threads: tens of thousands req/s, limited by downstream capacity and hardware, not thread count.

This is the **headline use case**.

sections.title: When CPU Work Enters the Picture
sections.content:
What if your request handler does **both** I/O and non-trivial CPU work (e.g., fetch data + complex transformation)?

Two options:

**1. Let it run on the virtual thread.** If CPU time per request is small (< 10 ms), carriers are fine.

**2. Offload the CPU part to a dedicated pool.**
```java
Executor cpuPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(
    Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors());

// On the virtual thread:
var data = fetchData(); // blocking I/O — virtual thread unmounts
var result = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
    () -> heavyCompute(data), cpuPool).join(); // CPU on fixed pool
return result;
```

**Heuristic**: if any task occupies a carrier for > ~10 ms of pure CPU, it's blocking other virtual threads. Profile with JFR; if you see long-running carrier monopolization, offload.

The cost-benefit: for mostly-I/O handlers, don't bother splitting. For clearly CPU-heavy slices, move them to a bounded pool.

sections.title: The Synchronized + ThreadLocal Audit
Downstream Protection — The Hidden Migration Risk
When to Adopt Virtual Threads
sections.content:
**Adopt eagerly when**:
- Building **new server-side Java 21+** code.
- Existing code uses thread-per-request and is bottlenecked by thread pool size (not CPU).
- Moving away from reactive frameworks that were adopted purely for scaling, not for backpressure semantics.
- Simple blocking JDBC + HTTP client code.

**Adopt cautiously when**:
- Heavy `synchronized` usage — audit for pinning first.
- Deep ThreadLocal reliance — plan ScopedValue migration.
- Downstream resources (DB connections, API quotas) — add explicit flow control.

**Don't adopt (or don't bother) when**:
- **CPU-bound batch jobs** — use `ForkJoinPool` or fixed thread pool.
- **Existing mature Netty/WebFlux systems** — they already work; migration cost > benefit.
- **Code with heavy native (JNI) calls** that pin.
- **Java 11/17 codebases** without LTS upgrade planned — virtual threads need Java 21.

**Hybrid is common**: virtual threads for request dispatch, dedicated platform-thread `ForkJoinPool` for CPU-heavy stages within a request.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **I/O-bound, high-concurrency workloads** — perfect fit: REST APIs, message consumers, outbound fan-out.
- **CPU-bound work** — no benefit; use traditional thread pool sized to cores.
- **Parallelism** is still limited by carriers (CPU count); virtual threads add **concurrency**, not parallelism.
- **`synchronized` + blocking I/O** pins the carrier — audit and migrate to `ReentrantLock`.
- **ThreadLocal** works but is heavy at millions of threads — consider `ScopedValue`.
- **Don't pool virtual threads** — one-per-task is the idiom; they're cheap.
- **Downstream flow control becomes your responsibility** — thread count no longer rate-limits; add `Semaphore` / Bulkhead.
- **Hybrid model** — virtual threads for I/O, dedicated platform-thread pool for CPU-heavy stages.
- **Spring Boot 3.2+** enables virtual threads with a single config flag.
- **Don't rewrite working Netty/WebFlux systems** just because virtual threads exist.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Virtual threads are the right tool for **I/O-bound, high-concurrency** workloads — not a universal replacement for platform threads.

**Perfect fits**
- REST APIs with JDBC and downstream HTTP calls
- Message consumers (Kafka, SQS) processing each message
- Fan-out outbound calls (1000 parallel HTTP requests)
- Thread-per-request web servers (Tomcat/Jetty with `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`)
- Any code currently bottlenecked by thread pool size rather than CPU

**Bad fits**
- Pure CPU work: image processing, parsing, encryption. Virtual threads don't add CPU parallelism — use a fixed pool sized to core count.
- Code with `synchronized` blocks wrapping blocking I/O. **Pinning** holds the carrier for the entire I/O; a few concurrent instances can starve all carriers. Migrate to `ReentrantLock` first.
- Code with large ThreadLocal state. Per-thread copies multiply across millions of virtual threads and blow up heap. Use `ScopedValue` for immutable per-scope data.
- Working Netty/WebFlux apps. The migration cost exceeds the benefit — they already scale.

**Mental model**
- **Concurrency vs parallelism**: virtual threads add concurrency (many tasks overlapping), not parallelism (many tasks computing simultaneously).
- Parallelism still = carrier count = CPU count.
- Concurrency = how many virtual threads fit in heap (millions on typical hardware).

**The migration audit checklist**
1. Find `synchronized` methods/blocks that perform blocking I/O — fix by converting to `ReentrantLock`. Use `-XX:+RecordJvmLoomPinning` via JFR to detect at runtime.
2. Inventory `ThreadLocal` usage — remove per-thread caching anti-patterns, migrate to `ScopedValue` for config.
3. **Add downstream flow control**: your old 200-thread pool implicitly limited DB concurrency. Now a million requests can hammer a 20-connection HikariCP pool. Add `Semaphore` or Resilience4j `Bulkhead`.
4. Size connection pools appropriately — they're your new bottleneck.

**Hybrid is common**
- Virtual threads for request dispatch and I/O orchestration
- Dedicated `ForkJoinPool` sized to cores for CPU-heavy slices within a request
- Offload with `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(cpuTask, cpuPool).join()` on the virtual thread

**The thread-pool-sizing calculation disappears**
- No more "cores × (1 + wait/compute)" math
- No more choosing between 50, 200, or 500 threads
- Just `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`
- Sizing effort moves to **connection pools and Semaphores**

**Recommendation:** For any **new Java 21+ server-side project**, default to virtual threads via `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` or Spring Boot's `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`. For **existing platform-thread codebases**, migrate opportunistically — audit for `synchronized`+I/O and ThreadLocal footprint first, and add explicit downstream flow control via `Semaphore` before flipping the switch. For **CPU-bound work**, keep using traditional thread pools — virtual threads don't change physics. Virtual threads are not magic; they're a focused tool that eliminates the I/O-scaling pain of traditional thread-per-request, letting you write simple, readable code instead of reactive chains for the 80% case.

questions.question: What is virtual thread pinning in Java 21 and how do you avoid it?
questions.title: Virtual Thread Pinning — Causes, Detection, Fixes
questions.direct_answer: **Pinning** is when a virtual thread **cannot be unmounted** from its carrier — usually because it's inside a **`synchronized` block** or executing a **native (JNI) frame**. While pinned, any blocking I/O holds the carrier thread, defeating the whole point of Loom. If many virtual threads pin simultaneously on blocking I/O, carriers get **exhausted**: no virtual thread can run because there's no free carrier. The two main fixes: **(1) replace `synchronized` with `ReentrantLock`** — it uses `LockSupport.park` under the hood, which does unmount correctly; **(2) minimize native calls** that block. Detection: JFR events **`jdk.VirtualThreadPinned`** or the JVM flag **`-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full`**. Future Java versions (JEP 491, post-21) plan to eliminate pinning on `synchronized` entirely, but until then audit your codebase before migrating to virtual threads at scale.

sections.title: What Pinning Is and Why It's Dangerous
sections.content:
Virtual threads are supposed to **unmount** from their carrier thread whenever they hit blocking I/O, freeing the carrier for another virtual thread. Pinning breaks that contract.

A virtual thread is **pinned** — cannot be unmounted — when:

1. **Inside a `synchronized` method or block.** The JVM's monitor lock mechanism is tied to the OS thread (carrier); the stack can't be parked while the monitor is held.
2. **Executing a native (JNI) frame** on the stack. Native code doesn't know about Loom's continuation mechanism, so the stack can't be captured.

If a pinned virtual thread hits blocking I/O, the carrier **sits idle waiting** with it — can't serve other virtual threads.

**Failure mode**: carrier exhaustion. If your pinned virtual threads ≥ number of carriers (= CPU count by default), **no other virtual thread can run**. The system appears hung or extremely slow even though nothing is actually doing work — it's the async-framework blocking-on-event-loop nightmare all over again.

**Critical insight**: under light load, pinning is invisible. It only bites under high concurrency when many virtual threads pin simultaneously. That's why **you must audit before rolling out to production**.

sections.title: The Classic Pinning Bug
The Fix — ReentrantLock
Detecting Pinning in Production
sections.content:
Three detection mechanisms, increasing in power:

**1. JVM flag (quick start)**:
```bash
java -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short MyApp
# or for full stack traces
java -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full MyApp
```
When a virtual thread would have unmounted but is pinned, a stack trace is printed to stdout. `short` shows just the pinned-relevant frames; `full` shows everything.

Use this in **staging and load tests**. Output is verbose under heavy pinning — use it to find sites, not as a permanent logging solution.

**2. JDK Flight Recorder events**:
```bash
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=app.jfr,duration=60s MyApp
```
Then open `app.jfr` in JDK Mission Control; look for the **`jdk.VirtualThreadPinned`** event. Shows how long each pin lasted, the stack trace, and the thread.

**Low overhead** — safe for production with sampling.

**3. Custom monitoring**:
A continuous JFR stream into your observability platform (Datadog, Grafana) can track pin duration and frequency as metrics. Set alerts on sustained pinning.

**What to look for**:
- Any pinned frame involving `synchronized` + I/O (database, HTTP, socket).
- Pinning during application startup is often benign (classloading) but during steady-state traffic is a red flag.
- Long pin durations (> 50 ms) on hot paths are priority fixes.

sections.title: Common Pinning Sources
sections.content:
**1. Explicit `synchronized` keyword** — most common. Search for it in code involving I/O.

**2. Libraries with internal `synchronized`**:
- **Older JDBC drivers** — some still use synchronized internally. Modern PostgreSQL and MySQL drivers have been updated, but verify versions.
- **`PrintStream` / `PrintWriter`** — `System.out.println` inside a virtual thread can pin during format/write. Usually fine for occasional logging; bad for high-throughput log lines.
- **`Random`** (the non-thread-local one) — synchronized internally. Use `ThreadLocalRandom` or `SplittableRandom`.
- **Some `Logger` implementations** — verify your logger version; modern Logback and Log4j2 releases are Loom-aware.

**3. Class initialization**: if a static initializer does I/O and two virtual threads race to trigger it, the JVM's class-init lock pins both. Avoid expensive class init.

**4. Native methods**: rare in typical business code; common in libraries doing compression, crypto, image I/O. Check for native-call hot spots with profilers.

**5. `Object.wait()` / notify()** — these also pin (they use the monitor). Use `java.util.concurrent` primitives (`BlockingQueue`, `Semaphore`, `CountDownLatch`) instead; all are Loom-friendly.

sections.title: The Future — JEP 491 and Beyond
sections.content:
**JEP 491** ("Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning"), proposed post-Java 21, aims to make `synchronized` blocks unmount-friendly by re-implementing the monitor logic using the same mechanism as `ReentrantLock`. Once it ships (targeted for a future LTS), the most common pinning source disappears.

**Native frames will still pin** — that's fundamental, since native code can't be interrupted by the continuation mechanism.

**Today's action items**:
1. Migrate `synchronized` to `ReentrantLock` on any hot path that performs I/O.
2. Track JEP 491's progress; when it lands in your LTS, a lot of the audit burden disappears.
3. Keep native-frame pinning detection in production monitoring.

**Don't panic-rewrite non-hot-path synchronized code** — a `synchronized` around in-memory operations that don't block is fine (no blocking I/O → no long pinning).

sections.title: Pinning Audit Priorities
sections.content:
**Fix immediately**:
- `synchronized` wrapping DB calls, HTTP calls, socket I/O on hot paths.
- `synchronized` in libraries you control where migrations to ReentrantLock are easy.
- `Object.wait`/`notify` in request-handling code — replace with concurrent primitives.

**Audit but may be acceptable**:
- `synchronized` around very fast in-memory operations (< 1 μs). Pinning still occurs, but duration is trivial.
- Class initialization one-off pinning at startup.

**Hard to fix — work around**:
- Third-party libraries with internal `synchronized`+I/O (old drivers). Options: upgrade the library, isolate the calls onto a dedicated platform-thread pool, or tolerate with more carriers (raise `jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism`).
- Native frames in image/video/crypto libraries. Usually fine unless those calls dominate.

**Watch out for**:
- **Silent slow degradation**: pinning doesn't throw errors — it just makes your service slow under load. Monitor pinning as a first-class SLI.
- **JDK version differences**: Java 21.0.1 vs 21.0.5 may have different pinning profiles; track JDK updates.
- **Increasing carrier parallelism** (`jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=200`) is a workaround but not a fix — it just delays the pain and wastes memory.
- **Thread dumps**: use `jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json` to get virtual-thread-aware dumps.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Pinning** = virtual thread cannot be unmounted from its carrier; blocks defeat Loom's scaling.
- Two main causes: **`synchronized` blocks** and **native frames**.
- **Failure mode** = carrier exhaustion: under load, pinning stalls the entire system.
- **Fix `synchronized` pinning** by migrating to `ReentrantLock` (Loom-aware via `LockSupport.park`).
- **Detect** with `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full` (dev/staging) or JFR `jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` event (prod).
- Common pitfalls: old JDBC drivers, `PrintStream`, `Random` (not `ThreadLocalRandom`), old logger versions, class initialization.
- **Short in-memory `synchronized`** is OK — pinning duration is trivial.
- **JEP 491** (post-21) aims to remove synchronized pinning entirely.
- **Native pinning** is fundamental — monitor and isolate hot native paths if needed.
- Audit critical paths **before production rollout**; pinning is silent until it breaks under load.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Pinning is when a virtual thread **cannot be unmounted** from its carrier, defeating Loom's scaling.

**Two causes**
- **`synchronized` blocks/methods** — the JVM monitor is tied to the OS thread; the continuation can't capture the stack while the monitor is held
- **Native (JNI) frames** — native code doesn't participate in Loom's continuation mechanism

**Why it's dangerous**
- If a pinned virtual thread hits blocking I/O, the carrier sits idle waiting with it
- Under load, pinned threads can equal or exceed carrier count
- Result: **carrier exhaustion** — no virtual thread can run, system appears frozen, CPU at 0%
- **Silent until it hits scale** — light load hides it, production load exposes it

**Classic bug pattern**
- `synchronized` method that calls JDBC
- Platform threads: serialized on monitor, 200ms waits, no big deal
- Virtual threads: carrier pinned during the 200ms JDBC; 8 concurrent = all carriers stalled
- Server appears hung; `jstack` shows all carriers waiting on DB

**The fix — ReentrantLock**
- `ReentrantLock` uses `LockSupport.park()` internally
- LockSupport is Loom-aware — triggers continuation yield
- Virtual thread unmounts cleanly even while holding the lock
- Migration: wrap with `lock.lock()` / `finally { lock.unlock(); }`

**Detection**
- **Dev / staging**: `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full` prints stack traces when pinning occurs
- **Production**: JFR event `jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` — low overhead, works with any JFR tooling
- **Custom monitoring**: stream JFR to observability platform, alert on sustained pinning

**Common pinning sources to audit**
- Explicit `synchronized` in application code
- Old JDBC drivers (upgrade to latest)
- `PrintStream.println`, `Random` (use `ThreadLocalRandom`)
- Old logger versions — upgrade Logback/Log4j2
- `Object.wait`/`notify` — replace with `BlockingQueue`, `Semaphore`, `CountDownLatch`
- Class static initializers doing I/O

**What's fine**
- Short in-memory `synchronized` blocks (< 1 μs) — pinning duration is trivial
- Occasional pinning at startup (classloading)
- Non-hot-path synchronized where upgrade cost exceeds benefit

**Future — JEP 491**
- Proposed post-Java 21
- Reworks `synchronized` monitors to be Loom-friendly
- Most common pinning source will disappear
- Native-frame pinning is fundamental and will remain

**Workaround for unfixable pinning**
- Isolate onto a dedicated platform-thread pool
- Increase carrier parallelism (`jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=200`) — band-aid, not fix
- Upgrade libraries to Loom-aware versions

**Recommendation:** Before rolling virtual threads to production, **audit every `synchronized` block on hot paths that does blocking I/O** and migrate them to `ReentrantLock`. Turn on **`-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full`** in staging under load-test traffic — every pinning stack trace is a potential production stall. In production, capture **`jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` JFR events** as a continuous SLI with alerts on sustained pinning. Non-hot-path synchronized code can stay as-is. Watch for **JEP 491** in future LTS releases — it will retire most of this audit burden. Pinning is the #1 reason teams roll back from Loom; treat it as a first-class operational concern, not an afterthought.
